4397.t: σάνδαλον (sándalon) + -ιον (-ion, diminutive), of uncertain origin, possibly loaned from Parthian, Persian, or another substrate of Asia Minor.

4389.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pterón, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ (“feather”). Related to πέτομαι (pétomai, “I fly”).

4303.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *kúklos, *kʷókʷlos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷékʷlos (“circle, wheel”).

4301.t: Uncertain. Possibilities include: * Metathesized from the Semitic root כ־ד־ב (k-ḏ-b) / ك ذ ب (k ḏ b) (Hebrew כ־ז־ב (k-z-b)) related to lies.

4328.t: Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀗𐀪𐀺𐀈 (mo-ri-wo-do), from an Anatolian word cognate with Lydian 𐤪𐤠𐤭𐤦𐤥𐤣𐤠 (mariwda, “dark”), from Proto-Indo-European *morgʷ-iyo-, from a root *mergʷ- (“dark”), whence also English murky and Russian мрак (mrak, “darkness”).

4332.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mólā, from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind; crush”). Doublet of μύλος (mŭ́los).

4315.t: Formation like μανδάκης (mandákēs) and καυνάκης (kaunákēs). Usually considered to be a Gaulish word, with cognates in Latin monīle (“necklace, collar”) and Proto-Germanic *manją (“collar”).

4316.t: Uncertain. One proposed etymology maintains that the verb derived from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥n̥-ye-ti, a denominative in *-yeti to a nasal-infixed form of the root Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to die”).

4391.t: A nominalization of the verb πήγνυμι (pḗgnumi, “to stick, fasten, build, fix”), meaning "that what is built or fixed"; see also πάγη (págē, “snare, trap”) and Latin pagus.

4377.t: From προδίδωμι (prodídōmi, “to betray”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent-noun suffix).

4329.t: Perhaps from Pre-Greek. Compare also μάχαιρα (mákhaira, “large sword”).

4393.t: Uncertain: Compare Sanskrit परशु (paraśú, “axe”) and Ossetian фӕрӕт (færæt, “axe”), pointing to a late, dialectal Proto-Indo-European word like *peleḱu- which does not appear to be a native formation.

4382.t: From προσέχω (prosékhō, “to guard against”) + -η (-ē, abstract noun suffix).

4337.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neyk- (“to attack, start vehemently”), cognate with Lithuanian ap-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), su-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), Latvian nikns (“bad, grim, vehement”), Albanian nis, and possibly Russian в-никнуть (v-niknutʹ),…

4346.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ksu-ró-s (“razor”), from *ksew- (“to scrape, sharpen, shave”). Exact cognate with Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšurás (“dagger, razor”); see also the verbal formation from the same root ξύω (xúō, “to scrape”).

4320.t: Uncertain; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *med- (“to measure”) or *med- (“to be full”), the latter comparable to Sanskrit मत्त (mattá, “drunk, intoxicated”).

4304.t: Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *káruks. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀏𐀬𐀏 (ka-ru-ka, accusative singular).

4302.t: Uncertain. Sometimes connected with κύαρ (kúar, “eye of a needle”) but according to Beekes of Pre-Greek origin.

4398.t: The formation is common to other technical terms like δοκίς (dokís, “beam”), ἀρίς (arís, “bow-drill”) and σελίς (selís, “crossbeam”) but the origin is uncertain.

4330.t: Explained by the ancients as deriving from μέλας (mélas, “black”), because of the soot which accumulates on the ceiling.

4347.t: From the root of ξύω (xúō, “to scrape, plane”) + -τός (-tós, adjectival suffix).

4351.t: From Proto-Hellenic *eworhéyō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wors-éye-ti (“to make it rain”), from *h₁wers-.

4370.t: From περι- (peri-, “around”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to make ready, to prepare”).

4335.t: From the same root as νεῦρον (neûron).

4357.t: παν- (pan-) + ἄγυρις (águris), Aeolic form of ἀγορά (ăgorā́, “marketplace”)

4300.t: From *κήρυγϳ- (*kḗrūgj-, stem of κηρύσσω (kērū́ssō, “to proclaim”)) + -μα (-mă, result noun suffix), from κήρυκ- (kḗrūk-, stem of κῆρυξ (kêrŭx, “herald”)).

4310.t: From λυτρόω (lutróō, “to ransom”) + -τής (-tḗs, “a suffix forming agent nouns”)

4343.t: Related to νύξ (núx, “night”). Beekes compares the suffix to one in Latin nocturnus.

4379.t: From προμάχομαι (promákhomai, “to fight in front”), from προ- (pro-) + μάχομαι (mákhomai, “to fight, do battle”); closely related to πρόμαχος (prómakhos).
